summary: Updates the HTTP/2 specification to forbid TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication, in the same spirit as the existing ban on TLS 1.2 renegotiation in HTTP/2. The goal is to avoid ambiguity about which requests a late authentication applies to. It was replaced by RFC 9113.

eli5.summary: When two people are already talking, nobody may suddenly ask for ID in the middle. This rule stops a server from asking for proof of identity partway through a web chat.

questions: can http/2 use tls 1.3 post-handshake authentication
how does tls 1.3 work with http/2
subtitle: Forbids servers from asking for client certificates mid-conversation over HTTP/2.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.3 supports post-handshake authentication (asking for a client certificate after the initial connection is established), but HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection, making it impossible to match a certificate request to a particular request.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8740 forbids TLS 1.3 post-handshake CertificateRequest messages when using HTTP/2, mirroring the existing ban on TLS 1.2 renegotiation.
tldr.outcome: HTTP/2 and TLS 1.3 work together cleanly. RFC 9113 replaced this document with a consolidated HTTP/2 specification.

facts.label: Applies
facts.value: Before and after HTTP/2 connection preface

today: RFC 8740 specifies an update to HTTP/2 that forbids TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication. This document was later consolidated into RFC 9113, the current definitive HTTP/2 specification.

sections.title: The Incompatibility
sections.content:
TLS 1.2 had a feature called renegotiation: partway through a connection, the client and server could restart the handshake to change keys or request the client to prove its identity with a certificate. HTTP/2 forbade this because HTTP/2 multiplexes many HTTP requests over one connection. When the server asks for a certificate mid-stream, the client cannot tell which of its pending requests triggered the request.

TLS 1.3 removes renegotiation but introduces post-handshake authentication, which serves the same purpose without restarting the whole handshake. RFC 8740 extends the HTTP/2 ban from TLS 1.2 renegotiation to TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication to avoid the same ambiguity.
sections.eli5: In TLS 1.2, a server could ask a client to prove its identity mid-conversation. TLS 1.3 has a new way to do this, but HTTP/2 still cannot handle it. This rule bans it.

sections.title: The Rule
sections.content:
HTTP/2 servers MUST NOT send TLS 1.3 CertificateRequest messages. HTTP/2 clients MUST treat such messages as connection errors of type PROTOCOL_ERROR.

This rule applies even before the HTTP/2 connection preface is sent. It also applies even if the client advertised support for post-handshake authentication (the post_handshake_auth extension) to another protocol like HTTP/1.1. The presence of that extension in the ClientHello does not indicate HTTP/2 support.
sections.eli5: HTTP/2 servers cannot ask for certificates after the handshake. Period.

sections.title: Other Post-Handshake Messages
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 defines two other messages that occur after the handshake: KeyUpdate (for refreshing connection keys) and NewSessionTicket (for resuming future connections). Both are allowed in HTTP/2.

The general rule is that post-handshake TLS messages are permitted unless they require interaction with the application layer (HTTP). KeyUpdate operates purely within TLS, and NewSessionTicket interactions are defined in RFC 8470 for early data. Both are compatible with HTTP/2.
sections.eli5: Other TLS 1.3 messages are fine. Only certificate requests are forbidden.
